1051.title: Christmas night
1051.hook: shepherds in the fields see the sky fill with angels (Luke 2:8–14)
1051.howItsDone: Luke's story of the shepherds is read in churches at Christmas, and some churches hold services late on Christmas Eve, where the angels' words are read and sung.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, and your line was better than a thousand months. Did the night get its minute of attention? Today, a second night of wonder, from a different book, told about a field. Day one thousand fifty-one.

Night shift. Not in a hospital or a warehouse, but out in the open, in a field, with a flock of sheep that can't be left alone. Somebody has to stay awake in case of wolves or thieves or a lamb that wanders. So a few men sit by the animals in the dark, wrapped in whatever they've got, talking low or not talking at all. Nobody important. Nobody expecting anything. That's where Luke's Gospel sets the night Jesus is born. Not in a palace or a temple, but out in the fields, with the people on the night shift.
screen: `NIGHT SHIFT, IN A FIELD.` → `NOBODY EXPECTING ANYTHING.` → `LUKE SETS THE SCENE HERE.`

segments.voice: First, who gets the news. The King James Version puts it simply: "And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." In Luke's story, Jesus has just been born in Bethlehem, and Luke's first announcement of that birth doesn't go to rulers or priests. It goes to men keeping watch over sheep. Second, the light. "And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid." Sore afraid means terrified. In this story, that's the first reaction to awe, and Luke doesn't hide it. Third, the message. The angel's first words are "Fear not," and then: "for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." Christian tradition hears in it the heart of Christmas: that the child born that night is the Savior, and that the news is meant for everyone, starting with the people out in the field. Then the sky fills. A crowd of angels appears, praising God: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." Fourth, what happens next, and why it matters. When the angels go, the shepherds don't stay put and argue about what they saw. They say to each other, let's go to Bethlehem and see. And they go. Notice something else too. Luke never says what season it was. The winter fields of carols and Christmas cards come from the time of year the feast is kept, not from the text. What Luke does give us is a dark field, ordinary men at work, and a sky that suddenly won't stay quiet.
screen: `THE NEWS GOES TO THE NIGHT SHIFT.` · `SORE AFRAID: TERRIFIED.` · `FEAR NOT. GOOD TIDINGS FOR ALL PEOPLE.` · `LET'S GO AND SEE.` · then, large: `GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to go outside on a winter night, or, if it isn't winter where you are, any night. For now, rehearse it. Sit back, and imagine the cold on your face, the dark around you, the sky wide overhead. Picture yourself as one of those people on the night shift: not waiting for anything, just keeping watch. Let the quiet be big. Then, sometime soon after dark, step outside for a few minutes for real. Look up. If you pray, you can say the angels' line, glory to God in the highest. If you don't, just keep watch, and see what the night offers. The bell holds the time.
Christmas night. Luke's dark field, where the first news of Jesus's birth comes to shepherds keeping watch by night. Today's word.
Your line: shepherds in the fields. Today, notice someone working a shift nobody thanks them for, and thank them. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: The mid-autumn moon
1052.hook: Chinese families gather to admire the full moon with mooncakes
1052.howItsDone: Families keep the Mid-Autumn Festival by gathering for a meal, sharing mooncakes, lighting lanterns and admiring the full moon; family members who are far apart sometimes call one another or send pictures of the moon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas night, and your line was shepherds in the fields. Did you thank someone on a thankless shift? Tonight's night of wonder has no angels in it, just a moon, a table, and the people around it. Day one thousand fifty-two.

Someone is cutting the mooncakes into wedges so there's enough for everyone, each one round, heavy, stamped on top with a pattern. Paper lanterns hang in the yard or on the balcony. Grandparents, cousins, the uncle who always arrives late. And then, at some point in the evening, everybody goes quiet and looks up, because that's what the night is for. Families across China, and Chinese families far from China, keep a festival in the middle of autumn that's built around one thing: the full moon, admired together.
screen: `MOONCAKES CUT INTO WEDGES.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS UP.` → `A FESTIVAL BUILT AROUND THE MOON.`

segments.voice: First, the shape of things. The Mid-Autumn Festival falls on a full-moon night in the middle of autumn, counted by the old lunar calendar. The moon is round, the cakes are round, and the family sits around the table. Roundness, tradition says, means being whole, being together, nobody missing. Second, the story people tell. There's a legend, told in many versions, of Chang'e, a woman who drank an elixir of immortality and floated up to live on the moon, leaving her husband on the earth below. So on this night, some say, she looks down from the moon, and people look up toward her. It's a story about separation, kept at a festival about being together. Third, the poets. One short poem by Li Bai goes something like this: moonlight falls by my bed, so pale I take it for frost on the ground; I lift my head and look at the bright moon; I lower my head and think of home. Another poet, Su Shi, wrote on a mid-autumn night while missing his brother. He ends with a wish that, though they're far apart, they might live long and share the moon's beauty together. Fourth, why it moves people. The moon gives the same light to everyone who can see it. Family at the table, and family who couldn't make it home, all look at the same moon at roughly the same time. The festival turns the sky into a meeting place. Awe, here, isn't a lonely feeling on a mountaintop. It's shared, passed around like cake.
screen: `ROUND MOON, ROUND CAKES, ROUND TABLE.` · `CHANG'E ON THE MOON.` · `LIFT MY HEAD, LOWER IT, THINK OF HOME.` · `THE SAME MOON FOR EVERYONE.` · then, large: `THE FULL MOON TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to share food under the moon. For now, bring someone to mind who you'd want at the table: someone near, or someone far. Settle, and picture the moon, wherever it is right now, above the place they are. The same light on their roof as on yours. Then, on a night when the moon is up, take something small to eat, a piece of fruit, a cookie, a cup of tea, and share it with someone outside or by a window. If they're far away, send them a picture of the moon. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If you don't, just let the moon connect you. The bell holds the time.
Zhongqiu. The Mid-Autumn Festival, where families look up together, eat mooncakes, and remember the ones who are far away. Today's word.
Your line: the full moon together. Tonight, look for the moon, and send one person who's far away a message: I'm looking at it too. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: The Perseid meteors
1053.hook: in August the Perseids streak across the northern sky
1053.howItsDone: People who watch the Perseids go somewhere dark on clear nights during the shower, lie back and let their eyes adjust; some Catholics in Europe connect the meteors with the feast of Saint Lawrence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhongqiu, the mid-autumn moon, and your line was the full moon together. Did anyone far away get a picture of it? Tonight the sky does something faster than the moon ever does. Day one thousand fifty-three.

Lying on your back in the grass at midnight is a strange thing for a grown person to do. The ground is cold. A neighbor's dog is barking. Sitting up, your neck ached from craning; flat on the grass, it finally doesn't. For a long while, nothing. Just stars, holding still the way they do. And then, out of the corner of your eye, a thin bright scratch across the dark, there and gone before you can point. Somebody next to you says, did you see that? And for the rest of the night, nobody wants to go inside. In late summer, in the northern half of the world, the Perseids are the reason people lie down in fields.
screen: `FLAT ON YOUR BACK AT MIDNIGHT.` → `A BRIGHT SCRATCH ACROSS THE DARK.` → `DID YOU SEE THAT?`

segments.voice: First, what you're seeing. A shooting star isn't a star at all. Astronomers explain it as a tiny piece of dust, left behind by a comet, hitting the air so fast that it burns up in a streak of light. They say the earth passes through that comet's trail around the same season each year, and for a stretch the sky is busy. The meteors seem to come from the part of the sky where the constellation Perseus stands, which is how they got their name. Second, another name. In parts of Europe the Perseids have been called the tears of Saint Lawrence, because they fall near the feast day of Lawrence, a deacon of the early church whom tradition remembers as a martyr. So the same streaks carry a Greek hero's name and a saint's tears, depending on who was looking up. Third, a psalm about names. People have given these streaks two names, one from a myth and one from a saint. A psalm in the Hebrew Bible goes further. In the King James words: "He telleth the number of the stars; he calleth them all by their names." In the psalm, naming the lights in the sky isn't only a human habit. Every one of them is already known by name. For people who pray the psalm, that's part of the wonder: so much light, and none of it anonymous. Fourth, the wish. Some people make a wish on a shooting star. Where that custom began isn't in any of today's texts, and it doesn't need to be. What it shows is a simple instinct: when something bright and brief crosses the sky, people want to answer it. A wish, a prayer, a gasp, or just a hand on the arm of the person next to you.
screen: `NOT A STAR: A SPECK OF DUST.` · `THE TEARS OF SAINT LAWRENCE.` · `HE CALLETH THEM ALL BY THEIR NAMES.` · `SOMETHING BRIGHT AND BRIEF, ANSWERED.` · then, large: `A SHOOTING STAR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look for a shooting star. For now, get ready for it. Close your eyes and let them rest, the way they'd need to rest in the dark. Let your shoulders sink as if you were already lying in the grass. Hold the psalm's line lightly: he calleth them all by their names. Then, on the next clear night, go somewhere away from bright lights, lie back or sit back, and give the sky some time. Shooting stars reward patience. If you pray, you can let the psalm be your prayer. If you don't, just wait, and watch. The bell holds the time.
Perseid meteors. Dust from a comet, burning up in our sky, named for Perseus, and called by some the tears of Saint Lawrence. Today's word.
Your line: a shooting star. Today, when something good and brief crosses your day, a joke, a kindness, a bird, answer it, before it's gone. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: Awe close
1054.hook: fifty-six days of looking up; awe, the traditions agree, makes us humble, though they name its source differently
1054.howItsDone: Some Jews and Christians read the book of Job, including God's speech from the whirlwind, as a picture of awe before the Creator; some readers of Emerson and some people with no religious tradition also seek the same humbling in nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Perseid meteors, and your line was a shooting star. Did something bright and brief cross your day? Today the block on awe comes to its last day, and we look back at all of it. Day one thousand fifty-four.

Fifty-six days. This block opened with a plain question: what is awe? Since then we've stood with Moses with our shoes off, heard a still small voice, read that the heavens declare, met Arjuna before the universal form, sat with Pascal in infinite spaces, and with Emerson as a transparent eyeball. Then we went outside: sunrises, clouds, one tree, water, storms, a newborn, a sacred building as a guest. These last days, a heartbeat, a sink full of dishes, an eclipse, and four nights of wonder. That's a lot of looking up. So what did it add up to?
screen: `WHAT IS AWE?` → `SCRIPTURES, POETS, SCIENTISTS.` → `FOUR NIGHTS OF WONDER.`

segments.voice: First, what kept happening. In story after story, awe did the same thing to people. It made them smaller. Not crushed. Smaller, the way a person can feel at the edge of the ocean. Second, the voice from the whirlwind, which asked Job about the stars on the night-sky day. This time, listen to how it begins. In the book of Job, after Job has demanded answers for chapter after chapter, God finally speaks, and the first thing God does is ask a question. In the King James words: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Job wanted an explanation. He's handed a question instead, and he comes out of it quiet. In Job's story, and in the Jewish and Christian reading of it, the source of awe is God. Third, the poet in the field. Emerson, standing on bare ground under an open sky, wrote: "I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all". In the same sentence he says the currents of the Universal Being circulate through him, and that he is part or particle of God: a God met in the woods and the open field, not a voice from a whirlwind. And some of the scientists we heard from found the same smallness with no God named at all: in the age of the stars, the length of time, the sheer size of what's out there. Fourth, the part that's easy to miss. In these two, the smallness isn't the end of it. Job is humbled, and then his story goes on. Emerson says he's nothing and, in the same breath, that he sees all. The traditions name the source differently, and they don't have to agree on it. But in these stories, the people who felt awe came back from it lighter, not crushed. Smaller, and somehow glad to be.
screen: `AWE MAKES PEOPLE SMALLER.` · `WHERE WAST THOU?` · `I AM NOTHING; I SEE ALL.` · `HUMBLED, AND LIGHTER.` · then, large: `SMALLER, AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look up once more. If you can, go to a window or step outside. If you can't, lift your eyes to the highest point in the room. Stay there. Let the sky, or the ceiling, be bigger than you for a minute. Let one moment from this block come back: a line, a night, a sunrise, a heartbeat. Don't choose it. Let it arrive. Then notice how you feel when you're the smaller thing in the picture. If you pray, you can give thanks to the source you believe in. If you don't, just stay with the size of things. The bell holds the time.
Universal form. Arjuna's vision, one of many names this block gave awe's source, each ending in the same humbling, lightening feeling. Today's word.
Your line: smaller, and glad. Today, when something makes you feel small, see if you can let it make you glad too. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: Six questions, looked back
1055.hook: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe
1055.carry: which one is quietly carrying you
1055.howItsDone: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes keep a journal and reread it at the end of a year; some synagogues read Ecclesiastes during the festival of Sukkot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, awe close and its universal form, and your line was smaller, and glad. That ended the last of this year's six blocks. Now the year itself starts to close, and the first thing to do is look back. Day one thousand fifty-five.

Six words could sum up this whole year: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Say them slowly and they sound like the chapter titles of a life. A person hurts. Someone they love dies. They love, and get loved, imperfectly. They spend their days working at something. They get wronged, and they wrong people. And now and then, the sky opens. This year asked each of those as a question, and handed it to the traditions willing to answer. Today, before anything else in the year's close, we line the six up side by side.
screen: `SIX WORDS FOR A YEAR.` → `CHAPTER TITLES OF A LIFE.` → `SIX QUESTIONS, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the questions themselves. Why do we suffer? What happens when we die? What is love? Why do we work? How do we forgive? And what do we do with wonder? None of these were asked to be solved. Each block brought voices from many traditions, scripture, philosophers, poets, scientists, and let them speak in their own words, each with its own name on it. Second, an old book that holds several of them at once. Ecclesiastes, in the Hebrew Bible, says in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven". And a few lines later: "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance". The writer doesn't rank the seasons. Weeping and dancing both get their time. In a way, that's what this year did: it gave suffering and awe, death and love, each a season of its own. Third, a poet's advice about questions. The poet Rainer Maria Rilke, writing letters to a young poet who wanted answers, told him to be patient with everything unsolved in his heart, and to try to love the questions themselves. Don't hunt for answers that can't be given yet, he said. Live the questions, and maybe, gradually, you'll live your way into an answer. Fourth, why look back now. A year of big questions can blur. Looking back doesn't mean deciding who was right. It means noticing which question you're still carrying, which one you put down, and which one is quietly carrying you.
screen: `SIX QUESTIONS, NONE SOLVED.` · `A TIME TO WEEP, A TIME TO DANCE.` · `LOVE THE QUESTIONS THEMSELVES.` · `WHICH ONE ARE YOU STILL CARRYING?` · then, large: `SIX QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to reread one note from each block. If you kept notes this year, in a notebook or on your phone, find one from each: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. If you didn't, let one moment from each come back to mind instead. Start now. Settle, and say the first word: suffering. Wait for whatever comes. Then death. Then love. Then work. Then forgiveness. Then awe. Don't judge what shows up, or what doesn't. Later, find the written notes if you have them. If you pray, you can offer each one up as it comes. If you don't, just let each have its season. The bell holds the time.
Six questions. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: the year's questions, each given its own season, none of them solved. Today's word.
Your line: which one is quietly carrying you. Today, pick the one you're still carrying, and say it out loud once, to yourself or to someone you trust. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: Which voice surprised you
1056.hook: a tradition you didn't expect to learn from
1056.howItsDone: People on a spiritual path of their own sometimes read across traditions and keep each teaching's source attached; some keep a list of teachers and lines they're grateful for, as Marcus Aurelius did in the first book of the Meditations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six questions, and your line was which one is quietly carrying you. Which one are you still carrying? Today we stay with the year, but turn from the questions to the voices that answered them. Day one thousand fifty-six.

A Stoic emperor on grief. A Sufi poet on love. A Zen saying about chopping wood. A psalm about still waters. A Sikh hymn, a Jewish blessing, a Hindu warrior on a battlefield, a Christian cook at a kitchen stove. This year put a lot of voices in one room, and maybe not all of them were ones you expected to hear. Maybe, somewhere along the way, one of them stopped you. A line you didn't see coming, from a place you didn't expect to learn anything from. Today is about that voice, the one that caught you off guard.
screen: `A LOT OF VOICES IN ONE ROOM.` → `ONE OF THEM STOPPED YOU.` → `THE ONE YOU DIDN'T EXPECT.`

segments.voice: First, a scene from the book of Acts. Paul, the Christian apostle, is in Athens, standing before a crowd of Greek philosophers. He's there to speak about the God of Israel and about Jesus. And in the middle of it, he quotes their own poets back to them. In the King James words: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." He found a line worth repeating in someone else's tradition, and he named where it came from. Second, why naming matters. Paul didn't pretend the line was his. He said: your poets said this. That's a small act of honesty, and also a kind of thanks. It's the same rule this path has kept all year: every teaching keeps its own name on it, and no voice is folded into another. Third, a man who thanked people by name. Marcus Aurelius opened his private notebook, the one we call the Meditations, with a list. From his grandfather he learned good character and an even temper. From his mother, generosity and simple living. From a teacher, to bear hardship and want little. On it goes, person after person, each with one thing learned. He never ranked them. He just named them. Fourth, what surprise does. Learning from a voice you expected to learn from can confirm what you already know. Learning from one you didn't expect can stretch you. It doesn't mean leaving where you stand, or changing who you are. It means someone from another room handed you something, and it fit. Today is a chance to say so.
screen: `PAUL QUOTES THE GREEK POETS.` · `YOUR POETS SAID THIS.` · `MARCUS THANKS EACH TEACHER BY NAME.` · `SURPRISE STRETCHES YOU.` · then, large: `THE SURPRISE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to thank it by name. Settle, and let this year's voices pass by in your mind. Don't search hard. Wait for the one that tugs a little: the line that surprised you, from a tradition you didn't expect to learn from. When it comes, name it, out loud or silently. Not just the line, but whose it was and where it came from, the way Paul named the poets and Marcus named his teachers. Then say thank you to it, in whatever way feels right to you. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own prayer. If you don't, a plain thank you is enough. The bell holds the time.
Marcus Aurelius. He named his teachers one by one in his notebook, the way Paul named the poets who surprised him from another room. Today's word.
Your line: the surprise. Today, tell one person about a line you learned from somewhere you didn't expect, and say where it came from. Day one thousand fifty-six.

1057.title: Teachers of the year
1057.hook: Job, Patacara, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse, Corrie ten Boom
1057.howItsDone: People on many paths keep their teachers close by retelling their stories, reading their words, and remembering them by name; some write letters to teachers they never met as a way of saying what they learned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus Aurelius, and your line was the surprise: the voice you didn't expect to learn from, thanked by name. Today the voices get faces, eight of them, lined up before the year ends. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Who would you hire to teach a class on hard things? Probably not a man sitting among the ashes, scraping himself with a piece of broken pottery. Or a young mother wandering a road with nothing left. Or a woman so ill the people around her bed think she's dying. Or a prisoner in a camp, holding on to one reason to get through the night. As a faculty, it's a strange one. Nobody here has a corner office or a quiet life to teach from. And yet, when this year's questions got hard, these were the people who did the teaching. Today we call the roll one last time: eight teachers, and what each one left on the table.
screen: `THE ASHES. A ROAD. A SICKBED. A CAMP.` → `A STRANGE FACULTY.` → `EIGHT TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: First, the ones who grieved out loud. Job loses his children, his wealth and his health, and he won't accept his friends' tidy explanations. At the end of the book, God turns to those friends and says: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." The one who argued is the one who spoke rightly. Patacara, as the Buddhist commentary tells it, loses her family and wanders out of her mind with grief. She meets the Buddha, comes back to herself, becomes a nun, and in time a teacher of others. Second, the ones who held on inside the pain. Julian of Norwich, in her showings, wondered why sin had not been prevented, and heard: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well." Viktor Frankl, writing after the camps, argued that one freedom can't be taken from a person: the freedom to choose an attitude. Neither of them pretended the pain was small. Third, the ones who loved and forgave without bargaining. Rabia of Basra, in a story people tell, walks with a torch and a bucket of water, to burn paradise and put out hell, so that God is loved for God alone. Kabir, in a verse kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says that where there is forgiveness, there is God. Fourth, the ones who made it small and kept it hard. Thérèse of Lisieux called hers a little way: no great deeds, just the smallest things, done out of love. Corrie ten Boom, whose sister died in Ravensbrück, writes in The Hiding Place of a former guard holding out his hand, and of taking it. Eight teachers from many paths, and each one stays exactly who they are. None of them was asked to agree with the others.
screen: `JOB AND PATACARA: GRIEF, OUT LOUD.` · `JULIAN AND FRANKL: HOLDING ON INSIDE IT.` · `RABIA AND KABIR: NO BARGAINING.` · `THÉRÈSE AND CORRIE: SMALL, AND HARD.` · then, large: `MY TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a letter one line long. Pick one of the eight, or a teacher from this year who isn't on the list, or someone in your own life who taught you the same thing without a book. Settle first. Let the face, or the story, come into view. Then write one line to them, the way you'd write inside a card: what you took from them, or what you're still trying to learn. It doesn't need to be clever. If you pray, you can hold that teacher in prayer. If you don't, let the line rest on the page while you sit. The bell holds the time.
Patacara. One of this year's eight teachers, Job, Julian, Frankl, Rabia, Kabir, Thérèse and Corrie among them, people in hard places who did the teaching. Today's word.
Your line: my teachers. Keep the line you wrote somewhere you'll see it today, and when the moment fits, tell one person about the teacher it's for. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

myth: at the end of the book of Job, God sides with the friends who explained his suffering
God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has (Job 42:7).
Rabia's torch and bucket comes from a verse of the Quran
it's a story people tell about her, not scripture.
Thérèse of Lisieux called her way a little way: the smallest things, done out of love
no great deeds; she made holiness small enough to fit an ordinary day.

fork.setup: you're one of Job's friends. he has lost everything, and he's angry at heaven. what do you do?
options: explain that his suffering must be punishment for something.
tell him to stop arguing with God.
stay with him, and let his complaint stand.
fork.reveal: the friends explained, and at the end of the book God says they had not spoken rightly, while Job, who argued, had.

original.note: Hebrew (Iyov): Job's name in the Hebrew Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: teachers are people who have the answers.
what it means: this year's teachers were mostly people in trouble: grieving, sick, imprisoned, arguing with heaven.
what a scholar hears: they reach us in different ways: Patacara through a commentary, Rabia through stories told about her, Julian, Thérèse and Corrie through their own books.
